clue.text: Industrial hand's mechanical aid — and diner's ?

definitions.meaning: a warehouse worker's powered truck with prongs for raising loads
what a diner does when bringing food to the mouth on a tined utensil

explanation.surface: A factory worker's machine is set beside something a diner uses, with a question inviting the link.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark asks what the diner's version is: the diner also raises food on a fork.
explanation.definitionFit: The warehouse truck raises pallets on prongs, and a diner lifts each mouthful on the table utensil with prongs.

clue.text: Logger in love

parts.note: in Shakespeare's The Tempest the prince who woos Miranda is set by Prospero to carry logs

explanation.surface: A lumberjack has fallen for someone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Logger' suggests a lumberjack; it is the young prince of The Tempest, made to haul wood while courting Miranda.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's prince in The Tempest is set to log-carrying by Prospero while he courts Prospero's daughter.

clue.text: Function of 1 across

parts.note: the job done by the warehouse truck at 1 across is to lift loads upward

explanation.surface: A cross-reference asks what the machine at 1 across does.
explanation.definitionFit: Lifting pallets upward is the whole purpose of the warehouse truck with prongs.

clue.text: Elizabethan city ?

definitions.meaning: Robert Dudley, Earl of this title, was Elizabeth I's favourite
a cathedral city in the English East Midlands

explanation.surface: A city from the age of Elizabeth I is asked about.
explanation.definitionFit: Robert Dudley held the earldom of that name under Elizabeth I, and the same name belongs to an East Midlands city.

clue.text: Can form a combine, to the detriment of our lighting

definitions.text: Can form a combine, to the detriment of our lighting

parts.words: Can form a combine, to the detriment of our lighting
parts.note: describes something able to melt and join, like the wire in a household fuse that melts and cuts the lights

explanation.surface: Firms merging into a combine harm the lights at home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Combine' looks like a business merger; it is the verb, to melt together, and the fuse wire that does so puts the lights out.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that can melt and join is meltable, as fuse wire is, and when it melts the lights fail.

clue.text: Sisyphus was such a self-assertive type

definitions.text: Sisyphus was such a self-assertive type

parts.words: Sisyphus was such a self-assertive type
parts.note: Sisyphus spent eternity shoving a boulder uphill, and a self-assertive person shoves themselves forward

explanation.surface: The Greek king Sisyphus is called pushy.
explanation.definitionFit: A pushy, self-assertive person shoves forward, as Sisyphus shoved his rock up the hill for ever.

clue.text: Jack of all trades ?

parts.note: read as the British flag's name paired with the body that groups workers of every trade

explanation.surface: A handyman who can turn a hand to anything.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jack of all trades' is a handyman; here Jack is the British flag, and an organisation of all trades is a trades body of workers.
explanation.definitionFit: The word goes before Jack to name the British flag, and also names a federation of workers in a trade.

clue.text: How much. ? Going, going gone ! (by 1970)

parts.note: an auctioneer's patter naming a price, and a British coin worth two shillings and sixpence, withdrawn in 1970

explanation.surface: An auctioneer asks for bids and brings down the hammer.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'Going, going, gone' is an auction call, but also the coin's fate: this old British coin of two shillings and sixpence was withdrawn from circulation in 1970.
explanation.definitionFit: This old British coin, worth an eighth of a pound, could be a bid price, and it ceased to be legal tender in 1970.

clue.text: Classic root

parts.note: the Latin word, from the classical language, for the root of a plant or number

explanation.surface: A traditional root vegetable is named.
explanation.definitionFit: Classic here means Latin, and the Latin word for root survives in mathematics for the base of a number system.

clue.text: Low current circuits lead to black out. Hell !

definitions.text: Low current circuits lead to black out. Hell !

parts.words: Low current circuits lead to black out. Hell !
parts.note: describes the river of the underworld, a deep current winding nine times round Hades

explanation.surface: An electrician curses as weak circuits cause a power cut.
explanation.walkthrough: Electrical words mislead: the 'current' is a river's, low because it lies in the underworld, and its 'circuits' are the loops it makes round Hell.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth the river of hate flows in nine loops round Hades, a dark stream in the realm of the dead.

clue.text: To Burlington House one fault's in the snapdragon dish

parts.note: the Royal Academy, RA, is housed in Burlington House in London
one is the Roman numeral I
read as faults, plural: moral faults are sins

explanation.surface: Someone at the Royal Academy confesses a fault concerning a party dish.
explanation.walkthrough: Snapdragon was a Victorian Christmas game of snatching dried grapes from a dish of burning brandy.
explanation.definitionFit: Dried grapes were the fruit snatched from flaming brandy in the parlour game of snapdragon.

clue.text: As is material for willin' Ted

definitions.text: As is material for willin' Ted

parts.words: As is material for willin' Ted
parts.note: a cloth woven with diagonal ribs is described, while read as a letter T plus willed it suits a willing Ted

explanation.surface: Cloth is chosen for an eager man named Ted.
explanation.walkthrough: The word splits as T plus willed: Ted, being willin', has 'willed', and his initial T goes in front.
explanation.definitionFit: Cloth woven with diagonal ribs, such as serge or denim, is described with this word.

clue.text: Peace personified

parts.note: the Greek goddess who stood for peace

explanation.surface: Someone is the very picture of calm.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek religion the goddess of peace bore this name, which also became a girl's name.

clue.text: Not out-and-out glove and helm characters

parts.note: to box is to fight wearing gloves
taken as written
to cox a boat is to steer it, to take the helm

explanation.surface: A boxer and an oarsman are named as figures who are not wholly out.
explanation.walkthrough: The two lodgers in J. M. Morton's farce share one room in shifts, one out while the other is in, so they are never both out: 'Not out-and-out'.
explanation.definitionFit: The two lodgers of a Victorian farce, sharing a room by day and night shifts, are its title characters.

clue.text: Attack-call the vet !

definitions.meaning: read as two words, a donkey is sick, which is a reason to call the vet

explanation.surface: Someone under attack shouts for the vet.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the word as donkey plus be unwell: a sick donkey is why one calls the vet.
explanation.definitionFit: To assault is a direct synonym, and split in two the word says a donkey is poorly, needing a vet.

clue.text: A component of branch-line rolling stock ?

definitions.text: A component of branch-line rolling stock ?

parts.words: A component of branch-line rolling stock
parts.note: a railway wagon part, read as a wooden beam from a tree branch on which wheels roll

explanation.surface: A part of a train used on a rural railway branch is described.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Branch-line' is railway talk; the real branch is a tree's, and the part is the wooden bar on which a cart's wheels turn.
explanation.definitionFit: The wooden bar on which a cart's wheels revolve is made from timber, so it suits a branch from a tree.

clue.text: Permissive climes ?

parts.note: regions of the globe measured by distance from the equator, and permissive freedoms granted

explanation.surface: Places with liberal attitudes are named.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both freedom of action allowed and the parallel bands of the globe, its climates or regions.

clue.text: Go slow

parts.note: to walk in a leisurely way

explanation.surface: Workers stage a go-slow.
explanation.definitionFit: Walking at a leisurely pace is going slowly.

clue.text: Comedian-endured claimant

parts.note: Little Tich was a famous Victorian music-hall comedian
borne means endured, put up with

explanation.surface: Someone claiming a right has been put up with by a comic.
explanation.walkthrough: The Tichborne Claimant was a Victorian impostor who claimed to be the lost heir to a baronetcy.
explanation.definitionFit: The famous Victorian impostor who claimed a baronet's estate is known simply as the Claimant of this family name.

clue.text: Ideal for pinching loaf sugar?

parts.note: an extending trellis of levers for grasping at a distance, read as suiting someone who loafs

explanation.surface: Something is good for stealing a sugar loaf.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Loaf sugar' looks like the old cone of sugar; 'loaf' is the verb, to idle, so the gadget suits an idle person who wants sugar.
explanation.definitionFit: An extending scissor-jointed grip lets an idle person pick things up without leaving the chair.

clue.text: Back a groovy ad for a narcotic

indicators.note: back tells us to read the whole string of pieces from the end to the start

parts.note: a groove is a rut
ad is short for advertisement

explanation.surface: Someone supports a hip advertisement for a drug.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back' turns A, RUT and AD round as one string.
explanation.definitionFit: The thorn apple plant of that name yields a poisonous drug causing stupor.

clue.text: See 14
Not only brave Horatius held the bridge spectacularly

definitions.text: Not only brave Horatius held the bridge spectacularly

parts.words: Not only brave Horatius held the bridge spectacularly
parts.note: Horatius held the Roman bridge, but clip-on glasses hold the nose's bridge as spectacles

explanation.surface: The Roman hero Horatius defended a bridge with style.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spectacularly' means in the manner of spectacles: these glasses grip the bridge of the nose.
explanation.definitionFit: Glasses with no arms stay on by pinching the bridge of the nose.

clue.text: It would be, to make a lion beg

definitions.text: It would be, to make a lion beg

indicators.note: to make these letters is to form them into a new word

explanation.surface: Forcing a lion to beg would be shameful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'make' asks for LION BEG to be made into a new word.
explanation.definitionFit: Humbling a noble beast would be base and dishonourable.

clue.text: Lit on Clio for a dance

indicators.note: the old-style signal that these letters stand for another word once rearranged

explanation.surface: Light is shed on the Muse Clio for the sake of a dance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for' asks for LIT ON CLIO to be reworked.
explanation.definitionFit: A lively French ballroom dance for four couples of the eighteenth century.

clue.text: Tapped, they're likely to turn out wet

definitions.text: Tapped, they're likely to turn out wet

parts.words: Tapped, they're likely to turn out wet
parts.note: barrels, once broached with a tap, pour out liquid

explanation.surface: People who are tapped for a job turn out to be feeble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tapped' and 'wet' sound like judgments on people; they are barrels broached for beer.
explanation.definitionFit: Barrels holding beer, once broached, run with liquid.

clue.text: 'Ye have scarce the soul of a ——' he said (Kipling)

definitions.text: Ye have scarce the soul of a

parts.words: Ye have scarce the soul of a
parts.note: the missing word in Kipling's line from Tomlinson is a tiny parasitic insect

explanation.surface: A line of Kipling's poem with a word missing.
explanation.definitionFit: In Kipling's Tomlinson the Devil scorns the soul as smaller than that of a parasitic insect.

clue.text: Why it's Philomela's nephew, so cut up

indicators.note: cut up asks for these letters to be chopped and rearranged

parts.note: the word why gives the letter Y, which is pronounced the same
taken as its letters, the apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: Someone asks why Philomela's nephew was chopped to pieces.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cut up' rearranges Y and ITS; it also fits the myth, in which Procne cut up her son and served him to his father Tereus.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth Procne's son, killed and served to Tereus, was the nephew of her sister Philomela.

clue.text: Large to revert to being narrow

parts.note: large means big

indicators.note: revert says the little word to turns back on itself

explanation.surface: A big person turns narrow-minded.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'being narrow' as a narrow being, a narrow-minded person.
explanation.definitionFit: An intolerant person is narrow-minded.

clue.text: Podiceps, perched on the back of an iceberg

indicators.note: the bird sits on the back of the word, read from the end backwards
the bird is perched inside the word iceberg, its letters sitting there

explanation.surface: A bird perches on a floating iceberg.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perched' finds EBERG in iceberg and 'on the back of' turns it round.
explanation.definitionFit: Podiceps is the Latin genus name of a diving water bird with lobed toes.

clue.text: In Suffolk, not by the Wash

definitions.text: In Suffolk, not by the Wash

parts.words: In Suffolk, not by the Wash
parts.note: a Suffolk market town on the Stour, which splits into soapy water plus inter

explanation.surface: A place in Suffolk away from the Wash, the bay on England's east coast.
explanation.walkthrough: The Wash is a bay on England's east coast; this town is far from it, but its name splits as suds plus bury, a wash and a burial.
explanation.definitionFit: A market town on the River Stour in Suffolk, birthplace of Gainsborough.

clue.text: Spring bathe of George's in Scotland

indicators.note: of says the bathing stream is made up around the short form of George

parts.note: a burn is a Scottish stream one might bathe in, as 'in Scotland' says
Geo is short for George

explanation.surface: A spring swim belonging to George takes place in Scotland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in Scotland' marks the burn, a Scots word for a stream, the place for a bathe.
explanation.definitionFit: To put out new shoots, as plants do in the spring season.

clue.text: The moon was Belloc's

parts.note: Hilaire Belloc wrote of the moon as a female relative

explanation.surface: Hilaire Belloc owned the moon.
explanation.definitionFit: Hilaire Belloc wrote of the moon as his female sibling in his verse.

clue.text: Youngsters always seen in the hirings

indicators.note: seen in says one word appears inside another

parts.note: lets are rentals, hirings of property
ever means always

explanation.surface: Children are always present when people are hired.
explanation.walkthrough: The youngsters are young hares, not children.
explanation.definitionFit: Young hares in their first year are called by this name.
